item.description: The Dutch, the British and the Americans took turns as hegemon not by blockading rivals but by getting them to stake their survival on someone else's maritime order — once they cannot live without the sea lanes and the markets, cutting them off becomes the most effective weapon short of war.
item.content:encoded:
The Dutch, the British and the Americans took turns as hegemon not by blockading rivals but by getting them to stake their survival on someone else's maritime order — once they cannot live without the sea lanes and the markets, cutting them off becomes the most effective weapon short of war.

Walter Mead breaks America's three-century winning streak into a five-step strategy and pushes it all the way to China, the Taiwan Strait and AI deterrence. What you get is a durable judgment framework, not news-cycle opinion.

4:47 Unpredictability is a form of power
‘Unpredictability’ is not madness; it is a modern strategy of power. Mead says post-Cold War American diplomacy used ‘let the whole world know where America's red lines are’ as its stabilizing pillar, while Trump profits by doing the opposite: crossing lines, threatening allies, turning commitments into bargaining chips. He saw through a secret of the information age — the marginal cost of lying: the first lie is expensive, the thousandth is nearly free. When Clinton was engulfed by the Lewinsky scandal, he discovered that shame only lives in other people's minds; as long as you keep walking, the dogs bark but the caravan moves on. Trump took that insight to industrial scale. The cost is borne by the American diplomatic system: when the world's number one power turns itself into the unpredictable card, every alliance and rule built on predictability after World War II is accelerating toward collapse.

10:00 The last step of global hegemony is cutting the cord
The Anglo-American maritime order did not win through some battle; it won through a five-step playbook. First, an open society on an island — the 17th-century Dutch tolerated heretics and Jews, and ideas and capital poured in. Then global trade: Dutch merchant ships went everywhere, and the wealth was so great that even the paintings are full of Turkish carpets and Brazilian parrots. Third, while continental powers fought over inland Silesia, you seized India and Canada worldwide. The fourth step is the riskiest: instead of copying Spain and sealing off your colonies, you invite the whole world in to do business, the British navy suppresses pirates, and every merchant ship benefits; Germany and Japan were likewise invited in after the war. Only the last step is the hole card: once the other side cannot live without your grain, your rubber and your shipping lanes, you cut them off — Germany discovered in World War I that Argentine grain and Malayan rubber had all been cut, and its economy promptly collapsed.

16:38 Everything China does is to avoid having its cord cut
Look at China through the same framework and you find Beijing is well aware of its own vital point. Mead says: suppose the mainland blockades Taiwan, and the US counter-blockades from a hundred miles off Taiwan's coast — oil cannot get in, manufactured goods cannot get out, soybean contracts with Brazil and Argentina are voided, and China's economy is strangled alive. He has discussed these things with officials and scholars at Chinese universities, and this worry is always present. So China's energy policy has to be read side by side: on one hand building oil reserves so large they surprise outsiders; on the other pushing hard on solar and hydropower while digging as much coal as possible. It is not schizophrenia, it is the same thing: pulling out, one by one, the soft spots of ‘dependence on the outside world’. He also warns the US not to retreat into isolationism — agriculture and AI both need overseas markets to keep themselves alive.

25:50 Every round of technology dividends needs new institutions to match
Mead starts from the ownership society: when America was founded it was full of independent farmers with land, and a bridge may be good but it raises my taxes — that trade-off is itself a political education. The railroad era was matched by the Homestead Act, with the government giving land to railroad companies and farmers, letting a national market grow; what replaced the family farm in the 20th century was the suburban single-family house, paired with tax-exempt municipal bonds and highways, becoming a new wealth-distribution machine. Now that machine has hit housing prices: young people cannot afford to live near where they work. His remedy is remote work and autonomous driving. When the commuting radius expands from 40 miles to 75 miles, usable land for housing rises with the square of the radius, and the physical space opened by technology is enough to carry two more generations. But the precondition is filling in the institutional ‘infrastructure’ — he coined the word info-structure, meaning the institutions and regulatory rules that let AI actually land in hospitals and courts.

40:22 Silicon Valley tilts toward the Tech Hamiltonian camp
American foreign policy debate has for centuries been four vocabularies: Hamiltonians want a strong state clearing the way for capital, Wilsonians want to spread liberal democracy, Jeffersonians fear a bigger government, Jacksonians are isolationist in peacetime and fight to the death when hit. The post-Cold War establishment was a marriage of Hamilton and Wilson, but Trump brought Jefferson and Jackson into the game. Mead says the new species truly worth noting is the Tech Hamiltonian. In the 1990s tech companies loved to say ‘we are a global company, Google has no borders, Washington has no say’; AI competition has turned tech into a contest of national destiny. Economic positions changed too: the old multinational car companies wanted borderless labor and markets, while Silicon Valley wants supply-chain and IP security, and even wants its employees to be patriotic, considers selling code to China shameful, and colleagues will report you outright. The core of business has shifted from old multinationals to tech nationalists — this is the underwater current of America's political realignment.

50:00 The power with more equipment fears technological turnover most
Mead has been to Ukraine twice. The first time he visited a drone factory and saw them converting children's toy trucks into ground drones carrying mines to blow up tanks; months later he went again, and the progress was unimaginably fast. The battlefield is now a gray kill zone, usually only two or three soldiers move together, and one of the hardest problems is ‘how to get the wounded out’ — you need to build a ground drone with a metal shield to drag people, with a squad of drones beside it hunting the enemy's drones coming to attack. He heard of one wounded soldier who took 63 days to be evacuated from the front. The changes flip every six months. The bitterest irony for the US: the power with the most tanks and aircraft carriers is precisely the one most afraid of this kind of parameter revolution — existing equipment turns from an advantage into a relocation cost. Russia's Black Sea Fleet has no great battle to fight, yet it is bottled up at home by Ukraine's small boats and drones.

54:16 The new variable most worth watching in the Taiwan Strait is Japan
On ‘will the mainland attack Taiwan’, Mead's judgment is that Beijing needs a very high probability of success before it is willing to cross the threshold — once it fails, it is catastrophic for the initiator. But between ‘attack’ and ‘do nothing’ there is a long gray ladder: for example requiring all merchant ships bound for Taiwan to first stop at mainland ports for customs clearance, or imposing a soft blockade, doing things sufficient to change facts on the ground without triggering an armed US response. The real new variable on the Taiwan chessboard is not America's attitude but Japan. The Japanese have already publicly concluded that if China takes Taiwan, Japanese independence is finished too; they are raising defense budgets, rewriting security doctrine, reshaping the national psyche. Historically Japan turns very fast when faced with a real threat. How steep Japan's learning curve is, and whether Beijing's calculus has to add Japan in, is the key to the Taiwan question in the coming years.

1:10:00 AI actually makes deterrence more credible
Moving Cold War deterrence logic into the algorithmic age, Mead points to a counterintuitive corollary: deterrence succeeds or fails on making the opponent one hundred percent believe ‘if I do X, you will necessarily do Y, and you can do it and are willing to’. As long as there is a human veto point in the decision chain — ‘I might soften when the time comes’ — that commitment has a crack. Automating part of foreign-policy decision-making to AI amounts to turning retaliation into an executable mechanism that will not hesitate — deterrence becomes more credible. But this is the doomsday machine problem from science fiction: decisions of civilizational annihilation no longer require a human to bear the consequences. His own assessment of the question is ‘very interesting and a little confusing’, and he does not think the answer has appeared yet.

item.title: ECT Is Not What You Think: A Century of Drift from Back Room to Routine Treatment
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-08-tpwky-ect-不是你想的那样-从密室到常规治疗的百年漂移/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-08-tpwky-ect-不是你想的那样-从密室到常规治疗的百年漂移/
item.description: Modern ECT is a procedure performed under anesthesia and muscle relaxants, with strong efficacy, but the evidence on memory-loss side effects is still incomplete, and social misunderstanding has left it over-stigmatized.
item.content:encoded:
Modern ECT is a procedure performed under anesthesia and muscle relaxants, with strong efficacy, but the evidence on memory-loss side effects is still incomplete, and social misunderstanding has left it over-stigmatized.

If your image of ECT is still stuck on One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest, this episode will overhaul it. Hear the actual procedure, the indications, the side effects, and one expert's clinical account.

8:07 What actually happens if you or I get ECT
If you or I were to receive ECT, the steps go like this: first a risk assessment and informed consent, then a physical exam, then an overnight fast. The next morning, in the hospital or an outpatient clinic, an IV line is placed and two blood pressure cuffs are put on (arm and right leg), with EKG, EEG and EMG hooked up. After the anesthesiologist puts you to sleep, the leg cuff is inflated to restrict blood flow to the right foot, then a muscle relaxant (such as succinylcholine) is given. Once the muscles are fully relaxed, a bite block is placed, and then a brief pulse of current is delivered through the electrodes (lasting seconds, or even half a second). The goal is not to make your whole body convulse, but to induce a generalized seizure, typically lasting 25-70 seconds. Because the muscles are already relaxed, you see almost no external movement — the whole thing is obvious on the EEG.

14:15 How the electrodes are placed, and why the right side first
There are several electrode placements: bitemporal (like in the movies), bifrontal, and most commonly 'right unilateral' — one electrode on the right temple, the other on the right side of the top of the head. Right unilateral is used for most people because it has fewer cognitive side effects. Why consider the right side first? Because for about 98% of right-handed people and 70%-90% of left-handed people, language function sits in the left temporal lobe. Avoiding electrical stimulation on the left side theoretically reduces language-related memory problems. But right unilateral is slightly less effective than bilateral. During treatment, doctors switch based on the patient's side effects and response: if bilateral side effects are too heavy, switch to right unilateral; if right unilateral isn't working well enough, switch to bilateral.

16:20 Seizure threshold and the effective dose
The seizure threshold is the minimum amount of current that can induce a seizure. There is no precise measuring device, so you start by estimating from age, then titrate up from a small dose until a seizure appears. But treatment isn't just about reaching the threshold — the effective dose is usually 2.5 to 5 times the threshold. With bilateral, 2.5 times is enough, while right unilateral needs 5 times, because unilateral stimulation has a harder time achieving the same effect. The dose varies from person to person, so it has to be adjusted by trial. If in one session a patient's seizure doesn't occur or doesn't last long enough (less than 25 seconds), the doctor may increase the dose and try again. Treatment is generally three times a week, with a full course of 6 to 18 sessions, sometimes longer.

20:22 We still don't know exactly how ECT works
Why does shocking the brain treat depression and catatonia? Frankly: we still don't fully understand. There are several main hypotheses. One is neurotransmitter changes: after ECT, serotonin, dopamine and GABA (an inhibitory transmitter) all change markedly. The rise in GABA is itself anticonvulsant, which could explain why the seizure threshold rises and seizures get shorter over a course of treatment. Two, large fluctuations in hormones such as ACTH, prolactin and TSH are seen in the hypothalamus and pituitary. Three, ECT promotes neurogenesis, with BDNF (brain-derived neurotrophic factor) as a key molecule. But how these changes directly relieve symptoms still has no one-to-one mechanism. The mechanisms may also differ across conditions (depression, schizophrenia, catatonia), so for now the only option is to keep researching.

24:24 Depression data: far better than first-line antidepressants
For treating severe depression, ECT's key data are quite strong: most studies report remission rates (symptoms fully gone) of 50%-60%, and response rates (marked improvement) of 60%-90%. By comparison, the best remission rate for SSRI antidepressants is only about 40%. ECT has another uncommon benefit — it can cut the 30-day readmission rate in half. This is not to say it should be first choice, nor that it has no risks (relapse or symptom rebound within 6-12 months is still not rare); but in patients with treatment-resistant depression combined with severe suicide risk, these efficacy advantages are hard to ignore.

26:27 Among side effects, memory problems draw the most concern
ECT's most difficult side effects center on cognition and memory. Right after the procedure there is brief confusion lasting from a few dozen seconds to half an hour, and for weeks there may be declines in attention and executive function. Interestingly, most cognitive functions actually improve in the long term — possibly because the depression improves. The real trouble is memory. Anterograde amnesia (difficulty forming new memories) mostly recovers within a few weeks after the course ends, which is why many people are restricted from driving or making major decisions during treatment. Retrograde amnesia (losing past memories) is what worries patients more: it usually affects recall of the most recent months or even years before treatment, and in most cases recovers, but in some it is permanent. Bilateral treatment is more likely to cause this problem than right unilateral.

34:55 Catatonia: a frequently misrecognized, fatal syndrome
Catatonia is often simply lumped in as a subtype of schizophrenia, but it is actually a psychomotor syndrome that any psychiatric or neurological illness can trigger. Patients appear awake, eyes open, yet are almost completely motionless and mute, and may show posturing or waxy flexibility (an arm placed in a position stays there and doesn't drop). Because they cannot eat or drink and don't move for long periods, they are prone to malnutrition, pressure sores, muscle contractures, and even death. Untreated catatonia has a mortality rate as high as 20%! The most common treatment is benzodiazepines, but ECT is extremely effective in catatonia from a variety of causes. The girl with anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis mentioned earlier (the 'Brain on Fire' case) developed catatonia, and neither immunotherapy nor lorazepam worked — in the end she recovered with ECT.

48:36 The biggest bottleneck isn't efficacy, it's access
Dr. Lopez believes the biggest obstacle ECT currently faces is finding a place to get treated. His hospital performs more than 6,000 treatments a year across two campuses, averaging about 10-12 sessions per patient. But it is not widely available across the US, and adults and children traveling across state lines for care are not few — especially in cases of infants, children and adolescents with catatonia from autoimmune encephalitis, where finding an experienced treatment team is extremely hard. So improving access is his greatest hope. At the same time, doctors on other internal medicine, pediatric and critical care teams often don't recognize catatonia and don't dare, or don't think, to call an ECT consult; so 'preaching' to non-psychiatric colleagues is also part of his daily work.

item.title: A Forgetful Kid Isn't Lazy — The Prefrontal Cortex Just Isn't Done Yet
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-08-asklisa-孩子丢三落四不是懒-是前额叶还没长好/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-08-asklisa-孩子丢三落四不是懒-是前额叶还没长好/
item.category: Ask Lisa: The Psychology of Raising Tweens & Teens
item.description: A 14-year-old boy's prefrontal cortex won't finish developing until 25, so forgetting things isn't an attitude problem. The real problem: parents whose own executive function is already stretched thin are supposed to build a system the kid can't possibly hold up.
item.content:encoded:
A 14-year-old boy's prefrontal cortex won't finish developing until 25, so forgetting things isn't an attitude problem. The real problem: parents whose own executive function is already stretched thin are supposed to build a system the kid can't possibly hold up.

This episode has medium information density, but it breaks ‘executive function’ into operable mechanisms: why an alarm is more reliable than memory, why a visual timer beats a phone, why you can't push a kid on something he doesn't care about. Suited to parents anxious about the back-to-school season.

5:12 The prefrontal cortex isn't done until 25, and not at 18 either
Tori defines executive function as ‘a set of behaviors and processes led by the prefrontal cortex,’ and the brain develops ‘from back to front,’ with the prefrontal cortex the last part to mature, not ‘fully cooked’ until a kid is in their twenties. So a 14-year-old boy still has ten years to grow. She specifically points out: we wouldn't expect any high school graduate to have executive function ‘fully wrapped up’ — an 18-year-old brain just isn't at that developmental level. But many parents assume that by 10th, 11th, 12th grade the kid should ‘have it all together’ — that expectation itself is wrong.

11:24 Parents have to catch their own guilt first, then talk solutions
The mother who wrote in said ‘I see myself in him’ and wondered if it was her fault. Tori says before giving advice you have to stop, because for many parents there's a string of scary questions behind this: Did I make him this way? Will this follow him his whole life? What will he be like at 18? She also reminds us to ‘hold two things at once’: for that boy, wearing the wrong T-shirt to the first practice is the end of the world, and that feeling is real; but in the big picture, this is the textbook definition of a ‘natural consequence’ — you didn't know to bring the jersey, so you have no jersey, it feels awful, and then we go back to the drawing board and figure out how to make this happen less often. Not bypass the discomfort, but turn the discomfort into fuel for building the system.

13:29 The system has to be simple enough to hold, with a safety net
Tori thinks of the system as ‘division of labor’: who's responsible for checking Google Classroom, who's responsible for checking the soccer team's app, while keeping a big safety net. If checking notifications is the son's job, the parent should still glance regularly to make sure nothing big slips through. Lisa shares her own approach: when her daughter ran cross-country in 10th grade, after getting an email from the coach she'd still yell from the kitchen, ‘Did you get this email?’ and wouldn't let it go until confirmed, sometimes just copy-pasting the content into a text to her daughter with a note, ‘Assuming you saw this.’ Tori says this trick is enough for kids without major executive function issues, but many families need a more fixed, more consistent way of checking.

15:30 Don't rely on memory — rely on a 6 p.m. Sunday alarm
Ideally you'd sit down at 3 p.m. Sunday to go through the coming week, but Tori says this ‘all sounds lovely until there's a soccer game at 2 p.m. Sunday, the 3 o'clock check time has already passed, and it never happened.’ So the second layer is the safety net: set a repeating alarm on your phone for 6 p.m. every Sunday, called ‘weekly check.’ If you already did it at 3, turn this one off; if you didn't, or something else knocked it out, this reminder tells you ‘before the week takes off, you need to do this.’ Lisa presses: so it's two slots on the calendar, 3 p.m. is the theoretical do-it, 6 p.m. confirms it actually got done, but 6 p.m. doesn't rely on memory — Tori says ‘I can't remember anything at 6 p.m. on a Sunday.’

16:30 There is no organization fairy, only lists and reminders
Tori and Lisa spent years counseling at schools and found some kids believe ‘the organization fairy will sprinkle some magic on me someday.’ Both of their reactions: No, dude, there is no organization fairy, she's not coming. The kids who look organized aren't organized because they remember everything — they have lists, planners, to-do lists, reminders. Tori says this gap is ‘what we forget to fill in for our kids’ — it's not a switch that flips on by itself. And the more distractions there are (an after-school job, caring for younger siblings, managing a chronic illness), the more you need a good, simple system to support executive function that's still ‘under construction.’

19:34 Three free tools: alarms, snooze email, visual timers
Tori starts with the things that cost nothing. First, the alarm function on your phone — she set six alarms that morning herself, one of them to confirm the carpool for her son's afternoon soccer game, because ‘our kids don't drive yet.’ She does a little check before taking the phone away at night, asking herself: ‘What is there today that I'm very likely to forget?’ Second, the email ‘remind me later’ function, made for those ‘mark this date, it's an October thing’ emails — you can't think about October now, so let it pop back up in three weeks instead of relying on memory to go dig it out. Third, visual timers, for ‘time blindness’: for people with a poor sense of how much time has passed or how long something takes, seeing time elapse visually is very helpful.

27:51 The tool that helps your kid focus is the one that distracts him
Lisa quotes Angela Duckworth: we generally don't put ice cream next to the broccoli. She asks: if I'm relying on the phone to keep my kid on track, but the phone is exactly the thing that most derails him, what do I do? Tori first admits adults are the same — you pick up the phone to set an alarm, get sucked into email, reply to the first text, and then ‘I spend my whole life asking: what did I come in here to do?’ She says asking kids to do this with an underdeveloped prefrontal cortex puts them at a disadvantage to begin with. Her solution is low-tech: a Time Timer, the kind with a red pie slice, battery-powered, with nothing on it that can distract you. Also, say your purpose out loud before picking up the phone — ‘I'm picking up the phone to set this alarm’ — to ground yourself and remind yourself there's only one task on this device.

30:58 You can't push a kid on something he doesn't care about
Tori explains why executive function is ‘uneven’: bandwidth is limited, impulse control is limited, and it drops when depleted, so the more important things in a day get attention first — work, picking up the kids — not returning the library books. But the hardest question is: what if this 14-year-old simply doesn't care about school and doesn't see the risk? Tori says first find what he does care about — say, playing soccer has a minimum GPA requirement, and you can't miss too many practices. Tie the requirement to what he actually cares about: if you want to keep playing soccer, here are the things we want to see happen, and here's the structure we'll build around you. The key is that this conversation can't happen in the heat of the moment when ‘he forgot about tomorrow's test’ — wait until everyone has calmed down.

item.title: Documentary director: there is no typical old age, only specific people
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-08-cn300980-纪录片导演说-没有典型的老年-只有一个个具体的人/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-08-cn300980-纪录片导演说-没有典型的老年-只有一个个具体的人/
item.description: Fan Shiguang, who shot two seasons of Qian Lang, says most marriages end up lukewarm or worse, and growing old together to the very end is rare. What we lack most isn't stories — it's money, and the habit of seeing old people as specific human beings.
item.content:encoded:
Fan Shiguang, who shot two seasons of Qian Lang, says most marriages end up lukewarm or worse, and growing old together to the very end is rare. What we lack most isn't stories — it's money, and the habit of seeing old people as specific human beings.

The first half is the two hosts talking, more feeling than fact; the second half is the director interview, dense with killed story ideas and behind-the-scenes detail — clearly the higher information density, worth starting at 41 minutes.

4:08 Five million in inheritance, and the law fights the deathbed wish
An elderly woman with no close family died in a Shanghai nursing home. While alive she had made a voluntary guardianship notarisation with notary Li Chengyang, but left no will. Sorting her belongings, the notary found she had left five million in assets, including a house, cash and bankbooks. She had said many times that she wanted to donate it to society and not give it to relatives, but that wish had no legal form. Li Chengyang ultimately chose to follow the law and look for statutory heirs, tracing through archives to children and relatives she had not seen in years. The notary office was itself divided, with colleagues arguing the old woman's wishes should simply be respected. The compromise was to propose to the inheriting children that 200,000 of the five million go to a fund helping old people with no one to rely on. The children agreed.

11:55 Whether they slept together decides whether the inheritance can be given
An elderly man with a terminal illness gave voluntary guardianship and his estate to a woman who had cared for him for years and was not a relative — while he had a biological daughter. The notary office debated this fiercely, and one key point was whether the two slept together: if they did not, the carer was merely a nanny or a live-in housekeeper, and an old man leaving his estate to his nanny was morally acceptable; if there was a sexual relationship, the matter stopped conforming to public morals. The carer was herself married, but had had no contact for years, so in effect the marriage did not exist. So it became an open-relationship question, and the notary office did not want to bear the risk of offending public morals on the basis of such a judgment.

16:02 Old people pairing up again increasingly skip the marriage certificate
Li Kangmei, the subject of episode two, was with Lao Li for eighteen years without ever registering the marriage, and there was no de facto marital relationship. The hosts found this far more common than they had imagined: when old people divorce or lose a first marriage, many choose not to marry when they enter a new relationship. They don't necessarily say they love the person; they say they want companionship, someone to look after them — behind it a fairly deep need against loneliness. Lao Li already had a terminal illness, and Li Kangmei's choice was whether to stay to the last moment or leave early because there was no de facto marital relationship.

24:46 Reality TV forces you to pick a side every five minutes
The hosts contrast documentary with reality TV: much of the tension in reality TV is manufactured, backed by a very strong narrative — knowing audiences look down on mama's boys, for instance, so a mama's boy is kneaded into the show. This destroys viewers' tolerance for the complexity of real intimate relationships: every plot beat, every five minutes, demands a position, and that position must be the morally correct one, then projected onto some character, and wherever that character goes you take his side. Documentary works the other way: it shows that no one has it easy, some characters get more screen time and some less, but you can see everyone's difficulty — and quite a few of those characters appear pixelated and anonymous.

34:20 The older generation says I sleep badly, not I'm depressed
Medical anthropologist Arthur Kleinman found that young people today have a rich psychological vocabulary and can quickly say I'm depressed, I'm anxious, I'm a bit bipolar; but older people, even when expressing psychological needs, still use somatised language — I've been sleeping badly lately, I have a bit of a headache — and won't say I sleep badly because I think too much, that I'm a little depressed. The hosts explain: in our culture it is easier to talk about physical pain, everyone gets a headache or a cold, there is no stigma; the moment you talk about depression or anxiety, it is a different order of stigma and pain.

43:53 The killed story: all she wanted was to play mahjong
Director Fan Shiguang tells a story he killed himself: the most diligent woman in a hospice ward, whose husband had bladder cancer and not long to live. She took the bus in at seven or eight every morning and left at five or six in the evening, like going to work, but you could see no love on her face — she just asked doctors and nurses again and again how much longer other people's family members had. Only later did it emerge that her son had died of a heart attack two years earlier; she was a shidu family, a family that had lost its only child, and her tears had probably run dry two years before. Someone asked what she wanted to do after her husband died, and she said play mahjong, because he had never let her play. The first scene shot after the husband died was her finding workers to smash the legs off a two-metre bed with a sledgehammer, one by one, and buying a mahjong table to put in that spot. The story was never used, because the team could not find her real inner world — they only had hold of part of the facts.

52:28 Growing old together is rare, not the norm
Fan Shiguang says the team did fieldwork sitting with roughly fifty families, across two seasons, and found that going from youth all the way to growing old together to the very end is not the norm but rare; most marriages are lukewarm, or worse. He tells of the first season's episode Lovers: an old man with Alzheimer's loses control and hits his wife, the daughter forcibly sends him to a specialised nursing home, and the old woman sneaks off to visit every few days, though the hospital won't let her come because it affects his mood. After the old man is sent to hospital, gravely ill, the old woman finally gets her chance to wait on him — cutting his nails, washing his hair, washing his feet. A month or so after he died, she said through tears: I looked down on him my whole life. When I was young I was a good student and he was a poor one, my family were intellectuals and his were workers, he insisted on courting me, and I had no way out, and in the end I muddled through a whole life with him.

1:04:18 Learning to drive at 95: one sentence strips away the right
Fan Shiguang says the team worked hard to break stereotypes, because people love to divide into groups and stick on labels — old people are like this, they've gone senile — and there is deep prejudice in that. In season one there was the story of a 95-year-old man learning to drive and taking the licence test. He caught himself saying, offhand, "driving is all very well, but he is 95 after all", and then asked himself: a 95-year-old, in that sentence of mine, has actually been stripped of his rights — that he doesn't deserve them. Public Security Ministry laws and regulations never said a 95-year-old cannot learn to drive, but in our verbal violence the right was stripped away. The episode's bullet comments were full of people saying can this old man really be allowed on the road, how selfish, what if he hits someone — all those worries rest on prejudice.

item.title: The Supreme Court Gave Students Constitutional Rights, Then Handed Searches and Paddlings Back to the Schools
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-stuffmissed-美国最高法院先给了学生宪法权利-后来又把搜包和体罚还给校园/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-stuffmissed-美国最高法院先给了学生宪法权利-后来又把搜包和体罚还给校园/
item.category: Stuff You Missed in History Class
item.description: From refusing to salute the flag to having a purse searched, six cases gradually drew the line of American public school students' constitutional rights; the Supreme Court laid down that "schools are not totalitarian enclaves" while accepting that corporal punishment and reasonable-suspicion searches do not violate the Constitution, and the boundary of those rights narrowed accordingly.
item.content:encoded:
From refusing to salute the flag to having a purse searched, six cases gradually drew the line of American public school students' constitutional rights; the Supreme Court laid down that "schools are not totalitarian enclaves" while accepting that corporal punishment and reasonable-suspicion searches do not violate the Constitution, and the boundary of those rights narrowed accordingly.

Each case gets five or six minutes covering the background and the holding, suited to listeners who want to grasp in one sitting the boundaries of speech, corporal punishment and searches in American public schools.

5:10 The flag-salute case: student rights enter the schoolhouse for the first time
Can students really invoke the First Amendment in class? This case actually begins with religion: Jehovah's Witnesses families held that saluting the flag violated the commandments against having other gods and against graven images, and refused to pledge and salute the flag. In 1940 the Supreme Court had ruled against them, and World War II pushed more school districts to require students to salute and recite the pledge daily. West Virginia expelled students who refused the pledge, labeled them delinquents, and their parents could face fines or even jail. In 1943 the Supreme Court overturned the earlier ruling 6-3, and Justice Jackson wrote the opinion on Flag Day: orthodoxy in politics, nationalism, religion or other matters of opinion is not to be defined by any official; students need not utter words they do not believe or make empty gestures. This was the first time the Court established that students hold some First Amendment rights inside school.

11:21 An official prayer text is held unconstitutional
In the Cold War the United States cast itself as a God-fearing nation, added "Under God" to the Pledge of Allegiance in 1954, and more public schools began reading scripture or praying before class. In 1951 the New York State Board of Regents asked religious leaders to co-write a short, non-denominational prayer, with each district deciding whether to adopt it. Districts that used the prayer let students opt out, but the parents of 10 students still sued. In 1962 Engel v. Vitale held it unconstitutional 6-1; the key was not whether it was compulsory but that the prayer was written by the government, which itself constituted establishing religion. Justice Black quoted Madison: it is proper to take alarm at the first experiment on our liberties; the same authority that could establish Christianity to the exclusion of other religions could easily establish one Christian sect. The ruling provoked fierce backlash, and the plaintiff families were mocked and harassed.

18:31 An armband is constitutional expression
In December 1965, middle and high school students in Des Moines planned to wear black armbands to class to protest American involvement in the Vietnam War. The schools announced in advance that refusing to remove them would mean suspension, and some students — including four siblings — wore the armbands anyway and were suspended. In 1969 the Supreme Court ruled for the students 7-2. The issue was that this was not ordinary dress or grooming but quiet, passive expression close to pure speech, and it did not disrupt class. Absent evidence of actual or demonstrable substantial interference with instruction, school officials may not suppress student opinion. The ruling said: public schools may not be totalitarian enclaves, and students and teachers do not shed their constitutional rights at the schoolhouse gate. This "substantial disruption" standard later became the baseline for free speech on campus. Justice Black dissented that students would from then on resist almost every school rule, and the host says on the show that this slippery-slope argument sounds pretty absurd.

24:40 A school-funded newspaper can be censored
In 1983 two pieces in the Hazelwood East High School student newspaper The Spectrum troubled principal Reynolds: a story on teen pregnancy that used pseudonyms but might still make the interviewees identifiable, and a divorce story that named and criticized a student's parent. Reynolds decided to cut both full pages rather than just remove the articles, on the grounds that there was no time to revise and the paper had to come out before the semester ended. In 1988 the Supreme Court ruled for the school 5-3. The key distinction is between "tolerating student speech" and "promoting student speech": this paper was funded and published by the school, readers would take its contents as endorsed by the school, and the two pieces were indeed ethically immature as journalism. The Court held that schools may exercise control over what they themselves promote. The rights established in Tinker thus acquired their first clear boundary.

29:46 Corporal punishment is not an Eighth Amendment matter
Host Tracy suddenly recalls that many of her childhood teachers kept wooden paddles on their desks, and on looking it up finds corporal punishment has still not died out in the United States. In the 1977 Ingram v. Wright case, the school's paddle was under two feet long, three or four inches wide and half an inch thick, with one to five swats in principle; but Ingram was struck more than 20 times in a single incident and needed medical attention. The Supreme Court did not dwell on whether that individual case was excessive, but held that school corporal punishment does not violate the Constitution. The reasoning: the Eighth Amendment protects the convicted, and prisoners are separated from schoolchildren by "the harsh facts of criminal conviction and incarceration"; schools are open places, with teachers and classmates as witnesses, and you can go home after school. According to NEA figures, corporal punishment remains legal in public schools in 17 states and is actually practiced in 14, and boys, Black students and students with disabilities are paddled at significantly higher rates.

33:52 Searching a bag requires only reasonable suspicion
In 1980 in New Jersey, a 14-year-old student, TLO, was reported by a teacher for smoking in the restroom. Vice principal Choplik searched her purse, saw cigarettes and rolling papers, kept digging, and found what appeared to be marijuana and evidence of drug dealing; TLO was ultimately convicted and given a year's probation. In 1985 the Supreme Court upheld the search 6-3. The ruling acknowledged that the Fourth Amendment binds school officials and that students have a privacy expectation, but that it must be balanced against the school's need to maintain a learning environment. So school searches need not meet the probable cause police require; the lower threshold of reasonable suspicion suffices. The teacher's report that TLO was smoking gave the vice principal reason to suspect she had cigarettes, and a purse is exactly the obvious place; seeing rolling papers naturally extended the suspicion to marijuana, which was equally reasonable.

item.title: To Make Criticism Land, Lead With High Standards and Trust
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-thinkfast-批评想被听进去-先给高期待与信任/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-thinkfast-批评想被听进去-先给高期待与信任/
item.description: Getting criticism believed isn't about opening with a few compliments — it's about letting the other person see that the standard is high and that you believe they can reach it. In one experiment, a single line — "the standard is high, but I know you can meet it" — pushed Black students' rate of actually revising their essays to the top.
item.content:encoded:
Getting criticism believed isn't about opening with a few compliments — it's about letting the other person see that the standard is high and that you believe they can reach it. In one experiment, a single line — "the standard is high, but I know you can meet it" — pushed Black students' rate of actually revising their essays to the top.

The originator of stereotype threat research breaks down the mechanism himself and grounds the intervention in a replicable experimental script. Twenty minutes of high information density, with none of the vague communication chicken soup.

1:04 Identity bias makes people underperform on the spot
When a situation carries a negative label about one of your identities, and that situation matters to you, you worry about being judged by that label. This worry comes from the situation itself: it depresses performance in tests, sports or intellectual tasks on the spot, and it also makes people avoid such situations over the long run, which in turn shapes who they befriend, where they live, and where they send their kids to school. The anxiety doesn't come from ability; it comes from the expectation of being defined by the label.

3:10 Social media lets labels chase you down
Social media's power lies in rapidly spreading sketches of what a group is like. People have no patience for the full picture and the exceptions, so it naturally multiplies the number of situations in which you fear being seen through your identity. Occasionally it also spreads images that reduce threat, but the overall tone skews negative. The result is that in a diverse society, everyone is more on guard about their own identity and about what others might be thinking.

6:16 A 15-minute self-affirmation exercise lifts grades
In racially integrated classrooms, Black students live with the constant possibility that their ability is being underestimated. Teachers asked seventh graders to spend just 15 minutes writing a short essay about the people and things they valued most. White students were barely affected, but Black students used the occasion to let the teacher know "I'm not just that label," and their grades began to rise — which fed a positive loop: better grades → less vigilance about the label → still better grades. The intervention cost almost nothing, yet it changed long-term trajectories.

9:20 Vigilance in diverse settings: remember or forget
The author calls this state churn. In settings where people of different backgrounds are together and the outcome matters, people are pulled back and forth between two options: remember that "others might read me through my group's stereotype" to protect themselves, or simply forget it, relax, and trust the person in front of them. This isn't fragility; it's real pressure generated by the situation. When the setting matters, it continuously drains attention that should be going to the task.

12:24 High standards plus trust make feedback work
In the experiment, students wrote an essay about their favorite teacher and received critical feedback. Under the first two approaches — giving it straight, or prefacing it with a "positive cushion" — white students trusted the feedback and Black students were highly distrustful. The third approach added only one line: "We have high standards, because these essays are going to be published; I read your essay and I believe you can reach them." Under that condition, Black students took their essays home to revise at three times the rate of the other conditions.

14:26 You can't assume others already trust you
After years as a dean and provost, Claude considers the most useful skill to be realizing that everyone you work with needs that signal of respect. Society's common mistake is assuming trust already exists, when in reality people worry about how you see the group they belong to. Truly effective leaders are good at giving that signal first: even if an employee disagrees with a decision, as long as they feel the other person respects who they are and their potential, the team atmosphere is completely different.

17:35 Let people see you're human before you talk trust
Claude breaks good communication into three things: first, let the other person know you understand what this situation means to them — when power is unequal, the person with more power has to send the safety signal first; second, near-obsessive clarity, because beating around the bush destroys valuable information; third, warmth and goodwill, because people need to confirm that the person across from them is a good person before they hand over trust. Matt sums it up as connection, clarity, care.

item.title: Latin Doesn't Make Surgeons: Exams Should Be Hard at Something Useful
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-econtalk-拉丁文练不出外科医生-考试难-不如考得有用/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-econtalk-拉丁文练不出外科医生-考试难-不如考得有用/
item.description: Latin doesn't make surgeons: skills barely transfer. If you assume "the harder the subject, the sharper the mind," a nation's brightest get wasted on the most useless knowledge — that is the lesson of the Qing examination system.
item.content:encoded:
Latin doesn't make surgeons: skills barely transfer. If you assume "the harder the subject, the sharper the mind," a nation's brightest get wasted on the most useless knowledge — that is the lesson of the Qing examination system.

It puts imperial civil-service exams, military selection and modern transfer experiments on a single chain of evidence, unusually connecting history with talent assessment — and the two sides genuinely clash.

10:03 Wrong exam content dooms the country, however smart the candidates
Hong Xiuquan failed the Qing examinations at least four times. After his last failure, he had a vision on the road home, believed himself the brother of Christ, and eventually launched the Taiping Rebellion — which Daisy says may be the deadliest civil war in human history, with deaths around thirty million. Hong was not alone among failures: examination seats fell far short of the number of candidates, many sat the exams into their forties and fifties without passing, and the only way home was to teach. Daisy adds that the deeper cost fell on those who passed: they were masters of the eight-legged essay yet knew nothing of the science and mathematics transforming the world. When the brightest young men can only practice a dead format, the country bleeds from both ends.

22:51 British civil-service reform was elites reproducing themselves
The Northcote-Trevelyan report is often seen by the British as the founding document of the modern civil service, but Daisy backs the revisionist judgment: in the name of a unified exam, it pushed Oxford and Cambridge classics graduates into key posts. Benjamin Jowett, master of Balliol, worked behind the scenes to place his classics students throughout the empire. Michael Coolican's "No Tradesmen and No Women" points out that the 1854 report reduced the most brazen buying and selling of offices, but also snuffed out the professional exams that departments had been growing. Exams can select people; what they test decides whether they select the worthy or select people like the selectors.

35:58 A bureaucracy without price signals corrects itself through corpses
Daisy attributes bureaucratic failure to the absence of feedback: no price mechanism, no profit and loss, so a department cannot tell whether its program saves or kills. The military sounds like a counterexample, but military bureaucracies err just as constantly in peacetime; almost every time Britain went to war after a long peace, the first year bred a crisis, as with the shell crisis at the start of World War I. What actually forces correction is not internal inspection but mass death on the battlefield. She calls it a crueler error-correction mechanism than prices. To make a bureaucracy reliable, you must first create a signal that shows consequences; otherwise no amount of rigor in selection can save the quality of everyday decisions.

43:06 The Royal Navy won by testing navigation, not Latin
Daisy notes that the true pillar of Victorian Britain was not the army but the Royal Navy. As early as 1677, after a run of defeats by the Dutch, Samuel Pepys set an oral exam for captains: three senior officers questioned them face to face on how to command a ship. Over the next century and more, navigation, charting and trigonometry entered the written exams, and chart-makers like Nelson, Cook, Flinders and Bligh passed through this gate. Daisy draws out two exam traditions: Pepys tested skills needed immediately; Macaulay and Northcote-Trevelyan later wanted classical languages. One served safety at sea, the other a layer of status — naturally the effects differed.

47:31 Content doesn't matter? Macaulay's screening argument misses the key link
Here comes the highlight: Daisy reads aloud Macaulay's 1833 parliamentary speech. The gist: whatever a age happens to teach, the best at it will necessarily be the cleverest, most industrious and most honor-seeking of the young; so Cambridge could teach Ptolemy instead of Newton and its top students would still be excellent; teach Cherokee instead of Greek and the best Cherokee scholars would still be the finest; even astrology and alchemy would do. Another MP praised it on the spot as the most practically wise speech in parliamentary history, but Daisy says flatly: this is eloquence running away with him, missing entirely that "what you learn really does matter."

51:21 Dead twigs and corn: wrong content makes discipline just watering
Daisy closes out Macaulay with the 1917 rebuttal of the American medical educator Abraham Flexner. Flexner said the devotees of mental training are like Egyptian priests: they stick a row of dead twigs in the soil and then water them on schedule for discipline's sake. Plant corn and the discipline is no less, with a crop thrown in. Against the American medical schools of the day, where many aspiring doctors were forced to read Greek and Latin before touching a medical book, Flexner's answer was: medicine is already hard enough, and using it to sharpen the mind is far more efficient than using dead languages. Daisy agrees: spend the best years of the most gifted on what has been disproven or is useless, and the winner will be the rival whose young people learn real knowledge.

59:21 Rectangles don't train triangles: transfer needs identical elements
Thorndike designed a cleaner controlled experiment: have people repeatedly estimate the area of rectangles until they clearly improve, then have them estimate the area of triangles — almost no transfer. Even for two shapes that close, the result holds, so the claim that classical languages sharpen the mind is even less credible. Thorndike's explanation was identical elements: transfer appears only when old and new tasks share the same components; far transfer essentially breaks down. Daisy draws the exam-design principle: to select people who can navigate, test navigation and trigonometry; to select people who can practice medicine, test medicine. An exam that truly works wires difficulty directly to the real task.

item.title: Global liquidity peaks: the companies that spent most aggressively on AI in H1 are discounted first
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-cn38ff4a-全球流动性见顶-上半年越激进砸-ai-的公司-越先被折价/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-cn38ff4a-全球流动性见顶-上半年越激进砸-ai-的公司-越先被折价/
item.description: A rising market needs new money to keep taking the other side. Global liquidity is already showing signs of peaking, and the companies that invested most aggressively in AI in the first half are shifting from being rewarded to being discounted.
item.content:encoded:
A rising market needs new money to keep taking the other side. Global liquidity is already showing signs of peaking, and the companies that invested most aggressively in AI in the first half are shifting from being rewarded to being discounted.

It puts US AI capex, Hong Kong IPOs and household balance sheets on the same funding chain — a macro framework that does not treat AI as a panacea.

0:33 A low break-issue rate is not a good signal
Do not read Hong Kong's low IPO break-issue rate as a strengthening market. In the first half of this year the break-issue rate was only in the teens, far below the roughly fifty-fifty level normal under a market-based mechanism — meaning the main participants in new listings are short-term speculative arbitrage funds, not long-term investors. Recently the supply of listed companies has shrunk, and IPO-related funds have blown up, yet the two newly listed companies still broke issue, showing that temporary control on the supply side has not solved the fundamental problem: Hong Kong faces the same peak in liquidity.

12:07 The more aggressive on AI, the sooner you are punished
Market attitude reversed within a single quarter. Before Q1, the capital market rewarded aggression: the louder the AI CapEx, the higher the valuation. By the time half-year reports were disclosed in late July, any large internet company that had made aggressive capital expenditure in the first half — especially those that spent their free cash flow to zero — was discounted, and even Google was not exempt. Q2 was precisely the quarter of maximum FOMO across the whole supply chain, with everyone afraid of price increases and spending money ahead of time; inventories could still hold up gross margins. By Q3, when inventories are exhausted and the price increases come back, the negative factors will show up together.

15:54 Nvidia is closer to Cisco in 2000
Nvidia's earnings look good, but its cash flow is changing shape. Before the dot-com bubble burst in 2000, Cisco rolled out "lease instead of buy" to help customers finance purchases, recognising future revenue early as sales revenue; Nvidia is now pushing lease-instead-of-buy as well. Free cash flow in the report halved quarter on quarter, and receivables on the books are far above historical levels — speculated to be partly related to the credit enhancement and collection structure that lease-instead-of-buy brings. Nvidia may therefore have reached a stage where it needs more aggressive financial engineering to sustain capital-market expectations, similar to Cisco's position back then.

33:21 Primary-market money comes from bullets loaded three years ago
The answer lies in when the funds raised. The money concentrated into AI and robotics from H2 2025 to H1 2026 mainly comes from funds raised at the 2020-2022 market peak; from 2023 to 2025 they barely deployed, until they saw state capital betting during a period when no one dared to invest and earning the most — the stories of ChangXin and ChangCun, two large models and two large chips stimulated market-based capital, and the mentality was: copy the state capital's homework. So this is not a rational long-term increment, but more like a delayed emotional release.

47:31 The new property policy detaches households from the funding chain
The key to recent real estate policy is not saving developers, but pulling households out of the old financing loop. Buying a pre-sale home used to mean the household played the role of financing object in the investment-driven chain: pay first, receive the home later; after the policy pushes the chain toward marketisation, buyers get completed homes and bear only the consumer role, with risk reset back to developers and financing institutions. The policy was introduced when prices were near the bottom in order to first stabilise the denominator on the asset side, avoiding panic from dismantling the chain during a decline. Japan after the 1990s and the consolidation of China's coal and mining industries both followed similar paths.

1:01:34 A slow bull is not a slogan, it is a chip structure
A slow bull does not rely on slogans; it relies on layering market chips by duration: at the bottom, low-valuation high-dividend blue chips taken up by insurers as long money that rarely trades; above that, public funds and index funds, performing a quasi-stabilisation function; above that, China Securities Finance and Central Huijin adjusting the index; and at the top, retail, private funds and active managers. The new insurance rules require liabilities and assets to match in term, return and liquidity — institutionally ensuring long money invests long, medium money medium, and short money short — and do not allow ordinary people's short money to be put into ten-year low-liquidity assets.

1:22:49 Crises get bigger with each rescue, and bubbles at least one and a half times
After the dollar left gold in 1971, global central banks became increasingly accustomed to intervening directly in crises by printing money, each time faster than the last. The quantitative easing after 2008 should have been cleared in a rate-hiking cycle, but was interrupted by political intervention, and then came the pandemic in 2020, so a larger flood of money was layered on before the previous bubble had dissipated — today at least one and a half bubbles have accumulated. Central bank governors have learned to print more money immediately when a crisis appears, and the endogenous result is inflation, rising financial assets and widening wealth inequality all at once. As long as the bubble is not allowed to clear, the world may face long-term stagflation in some form.

item.title: Central Banks Won't Kill the $100 Bill: It's a $2.5 Trillion Interest-Free Loan
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-oddlots-央行不愿废除百元美钞-那是一笔-2-5-万亿无息贷款/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-oddlots-央行不愿废除百元美钞-那是一笔-2-5-万亿无息贷款/
item.description: Cash use keeps falling, yet currency in circulation keeps hitting records. Central banks have every incentive to keep printing $100 bills: the money is effectively a $2.5 trillion interest-free loan to the U.S. government, and the price is convenience for money launderers worldwide.
item.content:encoded:
Cash use keeps falling, yet currency in circulation keeps hitting records. Central banks have every incentive to keep printing $100 bills: the money is effectively a $2.5 trillion interest-free loan to the U.S. government, and the price is convenience for money launderers worldwide.

It strips money laundering back from "bank wires" to watches, tractors, casino chips and VAT loopholes, and explains why central banks can't bear to kill the $100 bill.

5:09 The scale of money laundering hasn't moved in thirty years
The most commonly used estimate of money laundering is 2% to 5% of global GDP a year, which at today's roughly $100 trillion GDP is $2 trillion to $5 trillion. That figure comes from a rough estimate by former IMF managing director Michel Camdessus in the late 1990s, and nobody has come up with a better answer since. Oliver warns that the more alarming fact is that the ratio hasn't changed in thirty years: decades of anti-money-laundering action have not shrunk the criminal economy, only barely held it back from growing faster than the overall economy.

9:10 Banks spend $200 billion a year on AML for near-zero effect
When banks complain that KYC is too expensive, it isn't just whining. The U.S. passed the Bank Secrecy Act in 1970, and in 1989 the FATF turned anti-money-laundering into a global norm, forcing banks to hire compliance teams and install AI monitoring software. LexisNexis estimates global AML compliance costs about $200 billion a year — enough to solve world hunger and give everyone clean water. Yet the system generates a huge volume of suspicious activity reports every year, and launderers still stay ahead of regulators. The problem isn't that banks aren't trying; it's that the whole system is expensive, weakly feedback-driven, and almost nobody is accountable for the outcome.

12:14 Trade-based laundering is an order of magnitude bigger than cash smuggling
Cash smuggling makes laundering inside the banking system look small, but the bigger chunk never touches money at all: value is hidden in goods. About $25 billion in cash flows into Mexico each year, while John Deere and Caterpillar farm equipment exported from the U.S. becomes the consideration cartels get back; European luxury goods flow to China, drugs and goods are imported back in the China direction, and the triangle is settled with misinvoiced paperwork. Global Financial Integrity estimates this kind of trade-based laundering at about $1 trillion a year. A million-dollar watch worn through customs is far easier to move than a million in cash.

17:18 The Vancouver model: Chinese cash demand meets cartel supply
Chinese citizens can only convert $50,000 a year, while wealthy Chinese have plenty of demand to spend abroad. The Vancouver model matches that demand with the dollar cash supply from drug cartels: bags of cash outside Canadian casinos are handed to Chinese gamblers, the money is lost at the tables, and the gamblers run up gambling debts; that debt is offset on the other end in China by an RMB transaction and the drug sales that follow. Looked at as just the gambling, it looks like a loss; looked at across the whole chain, it's a triangular settlement that simultaneously repatriates cartel money and moves Chinese capital out. The model later spread worldwide, with luxury goods, consumer goods and drugs all serving as vehicles for moving value.

23:25 The VAT loophole lets the same goods extract 20% over and over
Zero-rated cross-border transactions in the EU were meant to keep national tax authorities from having to audit each other, but they became an ATM: goods entering the UK from Ireland don't owe VAT, and when sold to an affiliated shell company 20% is added; that shell company re-exports the goods back to Ireland and can claim a refund from UK tax authorities for the 20% it never paid. Round and round it goes, hence carousel fraud. The UK once largely suppressed it with a multi-agency crackdown, and the fraudsters then moved to continental Europe, where it now runs about €50 billion a year, spreading from Lithuania all the way to Portugal. Criminal organizations have no ceiling on cooperation: the more they cooperate, the bigger they get.

27:27 Nobody uses cash, yet central banks are printing record notes
In the digital payments era, cash is down to about 9% of transactions in the UK and about 13% in the U.S., so by ordinary logic the supply of paper money should be shrinking. After Bank of England governor Andrew Bailey raised the banknote paradox in 2009, the phenomenon only intensified: the value of UK notes in circulation doubled, and the U.S. is near $2.5 trillion. Central banks blaming it on "store of value" doesn't hold up — surveys show the average American adult carries only a bit over $400, while per-capita U.S. currency in circulation works out to more than $7,000. The Fed estimates about 65% of U.S. bills are abroad, but that just pushes the question past the border: nobody knows whose hands these notes are actually sitting in.

32:31 The $100 bill is a $2.5 trillion interest-free loan to the government
Seigniorage can't simply be understood as the profit from printing money: a $100 bill costs 9 cents, but it isn't "sold" to you — you can always exchange it back for goods at face value, so the cash the public holds is essentially an interest-free loan. With nearly $2.5 trillion in U.S. currency in circulation, the U.S. government gets interest-free funding equal to about 6% of the national debt; federal interest payments are now about 19% of the budget, and if that $2.5 trillion also had to pay interest, that would add roughly another percentage point. This is exactly why central banks don't want to hear anyone discuss abolishing cash.

47:51 AML incentives are inverted: the more reports, the less crime gets policed
Suspicious activity reports were born to be real-time intelligence for law enforcement, but reality is the exact opposite: banks hire thousands of compliance officers to fill out reports, law enforcement has no resources to read them, and most reports go into a black hole; a bank that misses one can face billion-dollar fines, while getting it right earns no reward. The side effects include debanking — large numbers of people who come under suspicion, many of them Muslim, get cut off from financial institutions. The guest's fix isn't to hire more compliance officers but to generate fewer reports, actually read them, and genuinely prosecute financial criminals — raise the cost of money laundering instead of drowning everyone in paperwork.

item.title: Russia Is Stuck in Ukraine, but Still Has Room to Open a New Front Against NATO
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-hiddenforces-俄罗斯陷在乌克兰-仍有余力对北约开新战线/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-hiddenforces-俄罗斯陷在乌克兰-仍有余力对北约开新战线/
item.description: Russia has not won in Ukraine, but attrition has forged the world's most advanced drone-infantry warfare experience; the guest argues it has ample capacity for a limited probe against NATO, and the window is the final phase of Trump's term.
item.content:encoded:
Russia has not won in Ukraine, but attrition has forged the world's most advanced drone-infantry warfare experience; the guest argues it has ample capacity for a limited probe against NATO, and the window is the final phase of Trump's term.

The guest is the Wall Street Journal's chief diplomatic correspondent and was in Kyiv on the day of the 2022 invasion; his judgments on Russian military capability and Europe's fractures are far more concrete than those of TV commentators.

19:16 Trump's anti-Europe talk may be taken literally by Putin
Everyone is guessing whether John Ratcliffe's secret trip to Russia was there to negotiate terms. The guest's judgment is that the visit looks more like carrying a message from Trump to the Russian side: don't take those on-air remarks about ‘America not caring about Europe’ seriously — if Russia invades Lithuania, Estonia or Finland, the US will send troops. The reasoning is that Moscow is bogged down in a war of attrition in Ukraine and badly needs to cut off European support for Ukraine, so escalating with a probe against NATO is one option, while Trump's earlier statements that ‘Europe is a bunch of freeloaders’ gave Putin room to misread, hence the need for a special trip to make the red line clear. One caveat: the guest does not have intelligence from inside that room; he is explaining why the account ‘makes complete sense’, not confirming it.

21:27 Russia's army isn't exhausted — it can still open a limited front
Russia has been unable to take Ukraine for a long time — does that mean it cannot open another front? The guest's answer is blunt: it can absolutely open a ‘limited front’ — not tanks rolling across Poland all the way to Paris, but making trouble in the Baltic direction, for instance blockading the narrow land corridor of the Suwalki Gap. He says the Russian and Ukrainian armies are the only two in the world today that fight modern drone-infantry warfare as a daily routine. The story of a 20-man Ukrainian drone team crushing an entire traditional battalion is widely told, but the Russian military has the same technology in hand: 20 Russians can likewise wipe out a NATO battalion that has not trained against drones. Outsiders assume Russia grows weaker the longer it fights, and overlook that it is also one of the parties being tempered by this technological revolution.

22:31 NATO might not even save Lithuania from Poland
A war game designed to simulate a Russian invasion of Lithuania led the guest to a deeply unsettling conclusion: even Poland did not send troops to save Lithuania, let alone other allies. The reason is not a lack of military strength, but that Russian forces advance too fast and nuclear deterrence hangs over everything, so allies fall into hesitation over ‘whether to enter’, producing a chain of waiting and watching. The guest says Moscow factors exactly this into its options. He also cautions that this is not quite the same as before 2022 — back then, more than a hundred thousand Russian troops massing could be clearly seen on the German and Belarusian borders, and there is no such material preparation yet. So the most immediate escalation may not be a conventional invasion, but small, ambiguous attacks that can be denied (hitting a warehouse or a drone first).

23:40 Russia is already probing NATO's limits with drones
At this stage, with no sign of a massed army at the border, Russia still holds a set of low-cost, low-attribution options: a limited strike on a NATO warehouse near Poland or Romania, or using a captured Ukrainian drone modified to create an incident, then watching whether NATO splits and whether the US steps in. The guest points out that such probing is already underway — an armed drone attacked a Ukrainian aircraft parked at Leipzig airport in Germany, and only a drone malfunction prevented deaths; Russian risk-taking is rising steadily, and the West has so far given no serious response. The senior European officers he has spoken with all believe the most dangerous window is the next one to two years, roughly falling in the final phase of Trump's term — the Kremlin will want to act before the US might let go.

27:53 Putin wants Ukraine disarmed, not a ceasefire
Would Putin accept a decent ceasefire deal? The guest's view is that you only have to look at what is put on the table: Russia has consistently demanded not just territory, but a cap on the size of Ukraine's army, limits on the types of weapons it may hold, and a cutoff of Western military aid to Ukraine. In his words, the goal is to make Ukraine ‘lose the ability to defend itself’; not neutral, but ‘castrated’, so that it cannot rise again in the next stage of the war — a year, five years or ten years later. Putin signed Minsk-1 and Minsk-2, and violated both. So the guest quotes the summary of Ukraine's former foreign minister: this war will end in one of only two ways — the end of Ukraine, or the end of the Russian imperial project. Waiting for the other side to change its mind is not on the menu.

31:08 Street protests can decide the fate of a wartime cabinet
Kyiv's recent personnel earthquake looks on the surface like an anti-corruption storm, but the key mechanism lies elsewhere: elections are frozen in wartime, and the president's legitimacy rests on a single ballast stone — ‘street support’. Zelensky initially fired Defense Minister Fedorov, who drove drone innovation, because he needed the backing of Commander-in-Chief Syrsky; after Fedorov was dismissed, Kyiv elites took to the streets, and the protests, small as they were, were enough to make the president reverse course — he removed Syrsky, brought in a younger general more popular at the front, and appointed a defense minister with a veteran intelligence background acceptable to all sides. Ukraine's independent anti-corruption bodies can still pursue people in the president's innermost circle, and when Zelensky tried to amend the law to absorb that body, he backed down within a week under street pressure. When elections are absent, the square equals the ballot box.

38:37 Resistance comes from memory, not heroism
Summing up Ukrainian perseverance as patriotic heroism misses what actually drives them. The guest says that after Russian troops take a Ukrainian town, one of the first things they often do is send bulldozers to tear down monuments to the victims of the 1930s famine — what they want to delete is a memory. Russian state television talks about how to ‘re-educate’ Ukrainians, making them forget their language and culture and become Russians. Around World War II the Soviets carried out a systematic purge of Ukraine's cultural elite, and in the guest's childhood he had no idea those writers existed, because collective memory had been erased. Ukrainians today are almost all descendants of survivors of that meat grinder of history, carrying the trauma in their bodies; it is precisely the fear of ‘never again’ that makes them prefer to die on the battlefield rather than return to that life.

45:59 Half a million veterans blocked the first wave of collapse
On the night of February 23, 2022, most people in Kyiv still did not believe there would be a war; the guest remembers knowing from his experience in Kabul and Baghdad that ‘impossible’ can flip overnight, but ordinary Ukrainians had no such reference point. What really kept the country from collapsing in the first days was eight years of war in the Donbas: that fighting was far from Kyiv, but it produced roughly 500,000 Ukrainians who had traded blows with the Russian army, and volunteer organizations evolved into a flexible, aggressive force. The psychological threshold had already been crossed in the Donbas — ‘we know what they look like, we know how to fight them’. Because of that experience, the swift collapse Putin expected did not happen, and the West's widespread expectations were wrong too.

item.title: A Child Hitting, Biting or Kicking Isn't Misbehaving — He's Reclaiming His Bodily Autonomy
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-parentmojo-孩子打咬踢不是坏行为-是在夺回身体自主权/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-parentmojo-孩子打咬踢不是坏行为-是在夺回身体自主权/
item.description: Stop asking how to make the hitting stop. A three- or four-year-old's hitting, biting and kicking is often the only tool left to shout "I have no say" after adults have taken control of nearly everything his body does — give some choice back, and the behavior shrinks.
item.content:encoded:
Stop asking how to make the hitting stop. A three- or four-year-old's hitting, biting and kicking is often the only tool left to shout "I have no say" after adults have taken control of nearly everything his body does — give some choice back, and the behavior shrinks.

Most approaches restate "no hitting" and add punishment, never touching the need that precedes the behavior. This episode treats aggression as a need signal, and shows the scripts and cases for negotiating with teachers.

4:21 A child who hits is shouting that he can't control his body
Preschool is often the first place a child is controlled in nearly every bodily arrangement by an adult other than his parents: where to sit, how to sit, when to speak and when to move. For the previous three years he could roughly decide when to run and when to use the toilet. Sitting on a rug for 20 minutes without moving is a real deprivation of autonomy; and a three- or four-year-old has no language to assert "my body is mine to decide," so hitting and kicking become one of the few tools still available. So when the call home comes, don't rush to lecture "hands to yourself" — ask instead: how much say did this child have over his own life before this, and what bit of it can be handed back now.

6:42 Kindergarten readiness is really obedience training
Teachers often say a given preschool has a high share of kindergarten-ready children, and the core definition of that readiness is compliance: sit down when the teacher says sit, even mid-task, even when the body is already overloaded. Parents fear that if the child doesn't comply now, he won't get into a good elementary school, college, a good life. But what the child pays for that definition is learning to suppress the feeling of "what I need right now." Teachers aren't villains either — they too need to feel competent, to keep children safe, to save effort, even to enjoy a taste of power; many went into education precisely to repair their own childhood wounds, yet only know the power-over kind of relationship. Only by seeing both sides' situations is there room to negotiate.

9:24 We grant ourselves regulation and deny it to children
If an adult at a party feels overloaded, he arrives early, leaves early, hides in a quiet room, even wears noise-cancelling earplugs — we find that entirely natural. Turn the camera on a child, though, and apart from conventions like extra exam time, we immediately worry that "too much accommodation will spoil him, he'll never survive the real world." The truth is that adults grant themselves far more regulation than they allow children. The source offers a concrete image: an adult stronger than you unceremoniously carries you out of the quiet room back into the middle of the loud party — with an adult, you'd instantly see it as a violation of bodily autonomy; when it happens to a child, we look right past it.

12:11 The repair point is before the behavior, not the behavior itself
Repeating "hitting is not okay" doesn't work, because that isn't the knowledge the child is missing. You need a different set of questions: what happened in the few seconds before this bite? What happened earlier that day? Is there a move or a new baby in the child's life? A sensory-overloaded child who gets jostled in line will melt down, so let him stand at the front, the back, or outside the line; a child who struggles with transitions needs a few minutes' warning. The adult analogy: when your partner snaps at you for no reason at night, it's usually not about that sentence but about the morning's argument, lost sleep, and a chain of stress. If the other person then tossed off "your attitude needs some work," you'd blow up too — yet that's often the only version we give children.

15:10 Talking to the teacher: don't assign blame, hear what the "no" protects
Telling a teacher "please change what you're doing" almost always hits a wall. A safer opening is to drop judgment and reconstruct the facts: don't look for who's responsible, just ask what actually happened; and list the family changes too, since that's context the teacher can't see. Once you know whether the child's trigger is sensory or autonomy, extend empathy to the three things behind the teacher: competence, the children's safety, and the relief of catching a breath. The request must land on a concrete, executable change, like "can he sit on a ball outside the circle." If the teacher refuses, the keyword isn't the refusal but what need that "no" is still protecting, and finding a different approach that satisfies both sides.

16:07 A naptime conflict, cleanly taken apart
