Jen's daughter Carys, at three, couldn't nap, but the teacher wanted her lying down; she was bored and frustrated — her need was to play; the teacher had two needs: state rules required offering a nap, and naptime was the teacher's own rest period. The solution they found was to move her mat to a slightly separated corner, where she could quietly play with soft toys that wouldn't roll, and the teacher could see her through the window from the break room. The child kept her right to free play, the teacher kept the rule and her rest, and Jen escaped the no-win cycle of incident reports. This segment shows that "negotiating by need" isn't empty talk: everyone gives a little, but everyone's core need is held.

17:53 Every method comes down to one question
Compress all of the above into one line: stop asking "how do I make the hitting stop," and ask "what need is this behavior communicating?" Hitting, biting and kicking are only surface signals; the real message may be "I need sensory relief" or "I need some say over my own body." Once the need is correctly named, a path to meeting it can be designed; and it is almost always the adult who changes the environment, because changing how the adult shows up is far easier than changing the child.

item.title: Thailand's Flood Wrecked the Hard Disk Drive Industry: The Biggest Factory Fell, the Number Two Took the Throne
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-06-asianometry-泰国洪水重创硬盘业-最大的厂跌倒-老二捡了王座/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-06-asianometry-泰国洪水重创硬盘业-最大的厂跌倒-老二捡了王座/
item.description: One flood in Thailand rewrote the hard drive rankings: the biggest player, Western Digital, saw shipments fall 51% quarter-over-quarter, while Seagate fell only 8% and overtook it to take the top spot.
item.content:encoded:
One flood in Thailand rewrote the hard drive rankings: the biggest player, Western Digital, saw shipments fall 51% quarter-over-quarter, while Seagate fell only 8% and overtook it to take the top spot.

What are the risks of geographic concentration in manufacturing supply chains? This flood provides a complete case study — industrial estate siting, zero inventory, and single points of failure all detonating at once.

6:13 Flood walls gave hard drive makers a false sense of security
The industrial estates were built on river floodplain converted from rice paddies north of Bangkok. For flood protection, developers installed ring levees up to two meters high, secondary wave walls, pumps and drainage systems; the parks quickly grew into small cities with their own housing and shops. But this engineering may have misled everyone. When the real flood season arrived in 2011, seven industrial parks were inundated within two weeks. Research later suspected that precisely this kind of seemingly complete infrastructure created a false confidence — the belief that even if it rained, everything would be fine. In other words, what manufacturers bought was not safety, but an illusion about risk.

8:24 Reservoir releases weren't the culprit — local rainfall was
After the flood, dam managers were blamed for releasing water too late, with criticism centering on favoritism toward farmers and rice-corruption allegations. But the research does not support this attribution. A 2023 simulation ran 17 scenarios swapping the release strategies of two dams, concluding that even with perfect foresight of subsequent rainfall, the flooded area could have been reduced by at most only 3.68%. Another 2020 study examined hydrological station data along the Chao Phraya River and found that in one low-lying disaster area, less than 30% of the floodwater came from the river, while 73.7% came from local rainfall. In other words, the water mainly fell directly on the disaster zone — reservoir decisions cannot carry the blame.

9:25 Why did Seagate, which wasn't flooded, also stop?
Seagate's factory in northern Korat was basically fine, but production still halted — because seven of its top ten suppliers were underwater. The typical case was Japan's Nidec, which makes spindle motors for hard drives and shut down directly after two plants flooded. The hard drive supply chain is interlocking layer by layer: no matter how safe the assembly line, if the motors don't come, the whole line stops. Seagate managed to hold its quarterly shipment decline to 8% by quickly qualifying new suppliers, modifying designs to reduce complexity, and negotiating payment terms with suppliers. In the same year, Western Digital's core plant took on water 1.8 meters deep, and quarterly shipments fell 51%. The difference between the two was not whose building was taller, but whose underlying supply chain could route around the break point faster.

12:34 Zero inventory amplified the flood into a global shortage
Before the flood hit, the hard drive industry had just completed a round of consolidation: Western Digital announced in March 2011 it would acquire Hitachi's hard drive business, and a month later Seagate announced it would acquire Samsung, barely bringing supply and demand back into balance. Precisely because there was no surplus inventory to draw down, the shock was multiplied. Tom Coughlin estimated that Q4 2011 hard drive demand was about 180 million units, while actual production was only 110 to 120 million; and the flood happened to hit right in the Christmas shopping season. Retail immediately raised spot prices by 20% to 40%, and a 1TB drive at Taipei's Guanghua Market went from NT$1,750 to over NT$3,000. Even Intel admitted in December that Q4 revenue would be about $1 billion short of expectations due to the hard drive shortage. A localized flood, transmitted through zero inventory, became a global shortage just like that.

15:41 The water receded, but hard drive prices didn't fall for two years
The water receded, but the shortage did not end quickly. Hard drive supply availability only returned to pre-disaster levels about nine months later; retail prices fell back even more slowly — hard drive prices on Newegg did not drop back to pre-disaster levels until April 2013. Backblaze did the math using its own purchasing records: in September 2011 the cost per GB was $0.044, and it would take until September 2013 to return to that level again. Why is it easy to raise prices but hard to lower them? The author lists several interpretations: the ecosystem recovered more slowly than expected, the two giants' 2011 acquisitions brought extra costs, tablets caused PC hard drive demand to permanently decline, and a more cynical guess — after Seagate and Western Digital acquired their second-tier rivals, only three major players remained in the entire industry, making prices easier to ‘stabilize’, or in his own word: cartelize. As for which one is the truth, he does not conclude.

18:47 The flooded giant chose to stay and keep building walls
Western Digital's post-disaster choice is telling: it did not retreat, but doubled down on defenses. WD and the Bang Pa-in estate owner built an 11-kilometer flood wall along the estate, and WD added a 6-meter-high inner wall around the factory; to add redundancy to its supply chain, it announced in December 2011 that it would build a new slider fab in Malaysia. A survey of 50 directly affected Japanese companies showed that nearly 80% decided to stay in Thailand. The reasons are not hard to understand: ready-made estates, supporting infrastructure and skilled workers are hard to pack up and take away. Thailand has since suffered multiple rounds of major flooding, especially in the 2020s when it happened almost every year; in November of the most recent year it even rained what was billed as a ‘once-in-300-years’ storm, but these estates have held out so far. Whether stronger defenses will be needed in the future can only be tested by the next major flood.

item.title: AI designs viruses that infect bacteria, but only 5% of the time
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-06-twiv-ai-设计出能感染细菌的病毒-但成功率仅-5/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-06-twiv-ai-设计出能感染细菌的病毒-但成功率仅-5/
item.description: For the first time, AI designed a complete viral genome from scratch that can infect bacteria; experimental validation puts the success rate at only about 5%, nowhere near as omnipotent as the media suggests.
item.content:encoded:
For the first time, AI designed a complete viral genome from scratch that can infect bacteria; experimental validation puts the success rate at only about 5%, nowhere near as omnipotent as the media suggests.

This episode takes apart the success rate of AI-made viruses, compensatory mutations and biosafety rhetoric, while demonstrating how an observational vaccine study can be falsified by an E-value.

12:43 A vaccine switch as a natural control
The trap in "healthy vaccinee bias" is that vaccinated people tend to be more attentive to their own health than unvaccinated people, so comparing the two groups mistakes lifestyle differences for vaccine effects. This study exploits the moment in 2017 when the US shingles vaccine switched wholesale from Zostavax to Shingrix: those vaccinated before the policy switch got the old vaccine, those after got the new one, and both groups were people who actively sought vaccination, so in theory the bias is erased. It is still not a randomised trial, however — socioeconomic status, smoking, diet and other unmeasured factors could still be unbalanced between the two groups, so it counts only as a quasi-experiment.

15:47 Weak confounding alone can overturn a vaccine benefit
How strong would unmeasured confounding have to be to overturn an observational conclusion? That is what the E-value measures. The E-value for this vaccine study is only 1.42, almost hugging 1, meaning a confounder that is not even very strong, one linked to both "which vaccine was received" and "cardiovascular outcomes", could explain away the observed risk reduction. An E-value needs to reach 3.4 or even 5 for a conclusion to count as solid; 1.42 is far from robust. The authors themselves concede that a randomised clinical trial is needed to confirm it, and that this observation should not be treated as evidence.

38:13 AI produces a functional viral genome for the first time
The researchers took the genomic language models EVO1 and EVO2 and had them write phage genomes: first the models read massive public DNA sequence datasets, then they were fine-tuned on PhiX174 to generate thousands of candidate sequences. Back in the lab, only about 5% of the products could actually infect E. coli — the first time AI has designed a complete genome from scratch that was then proven functional. If the media summarises this as "AI directly made a virus", it misses a key point: the model has only ever seen sequences, with no experimental annotation telling it which base does what, and the 5% hit rate shows how ignorant it still is about how sequence determines function.

44:37 The origin of replication is the model's most conserved memory
The prompt given to the model needed only the first 4 to 9 nucleotides of the PhiX174 genome for the accuracy of the output to rise markedly. The authors found that this unremarkable stretch is part of the origin of replication, and it was 100% conserved across every genome the model generated. It works like a password meaning "I am a real virus": the model treats the origin of replication as a core that must be locked down, and only dares to let other positions evolve. That also explains why such a short prompt works — what matters is not the prompt's length but whether it hits a functional pressure point.

56:55 Swap one gene and AI supplies 58 mutations itself
The design idea behind EVO36 was not to rewrite the whole thing but to swap genes: replace PhiX174's J gene with the shorter J protein from phage G4. When humans performed the same transplant by hand in the past, the product could not infect; but the AI's EVO36 infects normally, because it accumulated 58 additional mutations across the genome. These look like compensatory mutations that exist to re-adapt the foreign J protein to its local environment. Humans might not think to touch 58 positions at once, and this is exactly where generative models exceed the power of single-point editing.

1:00:15 Mixed phages specifically target resistant bacteria
Natural PhiX174 runs into a wall against already-resistant bacteria, failing to break through even after five passages; a mix of 16 AI-synthesised phages infected the originally resistant strain within one or two generations. Resistance is not broken by any single phage but by several synthetic phages recombining with each other and accumulating new mutations during replication, finally breaking the barrier through collective action. The result suggests that phage therapy should not bet on a single strain but should deploy multiple synthetic phages as a cocktail.

1:07:29 Don't call AI-made viruses an urgent threat
For that study generating PhiX174, a contemporaneous commentary used the word "urgent" to describe its biosafety implications. Vincent pushed back on that wording directly on the show: the authors had already shown through reproducible experiments that this kind of research can be done safely, so what is needed is not alarm-ringing but the start of building safety frameworks. He also stressed that as long as you have enough sequence, reconstructing a virus is not science fiction — precisely why frameworks are needed rather than fearmongering.

1:35:53 Not getting vaccinated is often just not knowing
Discussing the unvaccinated population, the article raises an often overlooked mechanism: some people do not get vaccinated not out of religious or ideological opposition, but because they simply do not know they should. Treating vaccine hesitancy uniformly as a "matter of faith" misdirects policy — for this group the key is not debate or persuasion but information outreach, so that they first learn the vaccine exists.

item.title: Sports Betting Is Seeping Into Gen Z, and the Regulatory Risk Is Underestimated
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-06-excessreturns-体育博彩渗透z世代-金融监管风险被低估/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-06-excessreturns-体育博彩渗透z世代-金融监管风险被低估/
item.description: Sports betting is becoming part of Gen Z's financial strategy; slow losses are harder to recover from than one big blowup, and it sits on the same platforms as financial products, with future regulatory risk widely underestimated.
item.content:encoded:
Sports betting is becoming part of Gen Z's financial strategy; slow losses are harder to recover from than one big blowup, and it sits on the same platforms as financial products, with future regulatory risk widely underestimated.

A multi-angle look at the hidden dangers of financialised gambling, from wealth management and market structure to regulation, with forward-looking value for understanding how the younger generation invests and where policy may change.

3:06 Gen Z treats betting as a financial strategy
A Betterment survey shows 26% of Gen Z investors see sports betting as part of a long-term financial strategy; in a CNBC survey, 52% of Gen Z investors moved money out of investments into sports betting over the past year. These numbers match Dave's experience with younger clients: betting has seeped into every layer of Gen Z and is now a problem wealth management has to face.

11:09 Slow losses are harder to recover from than a blowup
The insidious thing about sports betting is that dramatic blowups are rare; instead there is a steady drip of small losses — betting hundreds of baseball games over a summer, slowly losing 10% a week, occasionally winning 20% and feeling good, round and round. That eroding financial despair is harder to recover from than one big mistake; it amounts to a chronic tax on numeracy.

17:14 Regulatory risk is widely underestimated
Dave argues most people overlook regulatory risk because they assume regulators respond to catastrophic events, when more likely some future administration or state regulator simply says "enough." He points to Florida and Texas banning speed cameras first as evidence that regulatory moves are hard to predict. Companies depending on the current regulatory environment should be on alert.

21:14 Leveraged ETF products raise market-structure worries
In the same week, South Korea set strict investor-education thresholds for 2x leveraged products, Japan explicitly rejected single-stock leverage, and the US saw a filing for a 2x leveraged product that resets hourly. What worries Dave more is that the new ETF tries to hedge gambling risk using the futures market, but that futures market doesn't exist until the ETF has assets — the order is reversed, and it could divert resources from important financial participants who stabilise oil prices.

25:20 Tech giants' earnings show financial gimmicks
Cameron notes Nvidia extended receivables to help customers, while hyperscale customers extended payables to flatter free cash flow; Microsoft reclassified some capex into investing cash flow, lowering its capex guidance; activity inside SPVs doesn't show up on the statements. These "financial gimmicks" are common at cycle peaks — if the fundamentals were good, there would be no need for them.

29:24 Less disclosure worsens information asymmetry
Cameron opposes moving earnings to semi-annual reporting and cutting disclosure, arguing it worsens information asymmetry, benefits institutions with the resources to assemble information through the "mosaic effect," and reduces market efficiency. He also notes regulatory trends such as overturning the Chevron doctrine are concentrating power at the top, which is bad for innovation and competition.

38:27 The line between cultural appropriation and acceptance
Cameron criticises Urban Outfitters for selling Nirvana tie-dye sweatpants to 12-year-olds, calling it a lack of respect for the context, but Dave argues it could be a gateway to the music: even a kid who starts out liking only the smiley face might end up listening to "Heart-Shaped Box." The argument reflects the tension between gatekeeping and openness in cultural transmission.

47:35 Finding role models as an adult means accepting imperfection
Dave shares the story of Keith Morris defusing a conflict at a Circle Jerks show, which sparks a discussion about role models. Cameron notes that as people age they learn to appreciate others' strengths while accepting their flaws, just as they do with their parents, taking the good and leaving the rest. Dave admits he can't find a living role model because he knows no one is perfect.

item.title: Ion Drives: The Slow Rockets That Win Space
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-06-isaacarthur-离子推进-慢慢推-反而赢下太空竞速/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-06-isaacarthur-离子推进-慢慢推-反而赢下太空竞速/
item.description: Rockets aren't necessarily better the more powerful they are. An ion engine's thrust is as gentle as a sheet of paper, yet it can run continuously for years, accumulating speeds chemical rockets can't reach on a tiny fraction of the propellant — and becoming the workhorse of space logistics.
item.content:encoded:
Rockets aren't necessarily better the more powerful they are. An ion engine's thrust is as gentle as a sheet of paper, yet it can run continuously for years, accumulating speeds chemical rockets can't reach on a tiny fraction of the propellant — and becoming the workhorse of space logistics.

This episode covers ion propulsion's principles, limits and applications in full — good for anyone who wants a systematic understanding of why electric propulsion is now mainstream for deep space and satellites; those with no taste for engine detail can focus on the thrust and applications segments.

1:04 Ion propulsion wins on endurance
The rocket equation is cruel: to go faster you must throw away more mass, or throw it faster — but carrying more propellant makes the vehicle heavier, a tax collector's loop. Chemical rockets use high thrust to leave Earth quickly, but their exhaust velocity is capped by the energy stored in chemical bonds. Ion propulsion takes another route: instead of burning fuel, it uses electric fields to accelerate a small number of charged particles to extremely high speeds and throw them out. The thrust is astonishingly small, but it can persist for weeks, months or even years, ultimately accumulating a velocity change chemical rockets struggle to match.

4:04 Specific impulse and thrust can't both be had
Specific impulse measures how efficiently propellant is used; chemical rockets manage only a few hundred seconds, ion engines reach several thousand. But that efficiency rests on extremely low thrust: an ion engine can never lift off from the surface of Earth, the Moon or Mars — at most it can depart a small asteroid whose gravity an astronaut could jump off. It isn't physically impossible; it trades thrust for efficiency, and time for speed. Chemical rockets are sprinters, ion engines are marathoners.

6:07 Two mainstream forms of electric propulsion
The classic gridded ion thruster ionises propellant atoms and accelerates them out through charged grids — high efficiency, but the grids are continuously eroded. Hall thrusters use electromagnetic fields to ionise and accelerate propellant, with somewhat lower specific impulse but higher thrust, better suited to satellites, and they are the mainstay of modern electric propulsion. There are also micro electric-thruster systems for small satellites, and high-power plasma concepts — the core difference among all of these ultimately comes down to how to get enough electrical power.

10:13 Why xenon is the default propellant
Propellant choice isn't intuitive: at the same accelerating voltage, helium ions fly fastest and xenon slowest, but thrust depends on momentum — mass times velocity — so helium looks tempting. Yet at the same power, a higher exhaust velocity actually means lower thrust; helium needs about 590 megajoules to ionise a kilogram, xenon only about 9 megajoules. Xenon is an inert gas that doesn't corrode the engine. It is today's high-end choice for ion propulsion, but costs about a thousand dollars per kilogram. Argon is far cheaper and is the industrial choice of the future.

18:20 Slow rockets are the bedrock of space logistics
Ion propulsion is especially suited to missions already in orbit: spiralling orbits up or down, rendezvousing with low-gravity small bodies. Humans are impatient cargo, but supplies — water, metal, parts, propellant — don't care about being shipped slowly. A future Mars programme or lunar base could move people fast with chemical or nuclear thermal propulsion while ion engines deliver the cargo ahead of time, slowly. Machines do the boring work; the history of civilisation is written in freighters, ships, railways, trucks and shipping containers.

26:25 Longevity is the core requirement, not a bonus
An ion thruster must run continuously for thousands or even tens of thousands of hours; grids erode, cathodes fail, power processing units have to survive years of operation. A chemical engine burns for minutes, an ion engine for years — this isn't easier, it's a different direction in which things get hard. It also struggles to exploit the Oberth effect: a chemical rocket can burn hard and briefly at orbital perigee for a huge gain in orbital energy, while an ion engine's thrust is spread over months and loses that advantage for nothing.

30:26 Propellant isn't fuel, it's money
Propellant isn't just fuel; it is mass that must be launched, mined, processed, stored, transferred and protected. Every kilogram of propellant saved is another kilogram of instruments, shielding, cargo and lifetime. The key question of the early space age was whether you could reach space at all; the key question of the next era is whether you can move around in space cheaply. Ion propulsion won't get people to Mars, but it may be the crucial tool for building space infrastructure — exploration gets the headlines, logistics builds the civilisation.

31:26 A low-speed engine can build an interstellar civilisation
Today's ion engines can't fly interstellar missions within a human lifetime, but far-future electric propulsion — with megavolt or even gigavolt accelerators, enormous power systems and propellant measured in tonnes — would begin to approach an interstellar precursor vehicle. More importantly, even if ion engines never become interstellar drives, they remain key to building the infrastructure of an interstellar civilisation: before launching a starship you need to build collectors, mines, fuel depots, telescope arrays, habitats and shipyards. These must be moved, assembled, maintained and resupplied, and ion propulsion may be the best way to do that slow work. It isn't the starship engine itself; it is one of the engines that builds the civilisation that then builds the starship.

item.title: Companies Are Becoming a Series of Loops: AI Can Reach the Peak, but Choosing the Next Mountain Still Takes a Human
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-06-lennys-公司变成一串自动循环-ai-能到坡顶-换山还得靠人/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-06-lennys-公司变成一串自动循环-ai-能到坡顶-换山还得靠人/
item.description: Companies are being rebuilt as a chain of interlocking loops; loops can push the current business to a local maximum, but after the plateau, choosing the next mountain still depends on human intuition.
item.content:encoded:
Companies are being rebuilt as a chain of interlocking loops; loops can push the current business to a local maximum, but after the plateau, choosing the next mountain still depends on human intuition.

A structural judgment from an a16z partner: companies will be rewritten by loops, and the biggest opportunity in consumer AI is joy, not efficiency. The takes are often counterintuitive — good for stress-testing your own product roadmap.

4:05 The AI era will not replicate winner-take-all
The AI era will not play out the way mobile internet did, with winner-take-all dynamics: network effects once pushed search and social toward one or two players, whereas every layer of the AI stack now has roughly 20 relevant participants. Two years ago everyone thought coding agents would end up with a single winner; today Claude Code, Codex, Lovable and Replit are all moving forward at once. Anish says the people at the frontier inside the labs believe what is actually happening is autocatalytic effects — using new technology to improve your own processes — rather than recursive self-improvement, so there will be no runaway winner that swallows everyone. The takeaway for founders: don't bet on a single full-stack giant; every layer (models, agents, interfaces) still has a long-term place.

10:08 CEOs want to build bigger companies, not fewer employees
Employees probably don't need to worry too much about being replaced by AI — not because the technology isn't strong enough, but because a CEO's incentive is growth, not shrinking. Sundar doesn't want to run a more efficient $4 trillion company; he wants to build a $40 trillion company. A Google executive friend told Anish the company isn't laying people off but using AI to compress a two-year roadmap into three months, and the hard problem has become ‘what should we add to the roadmap’. When execution is no longer scarce, attention shifts from saving labor to finding new things to do for a bigger goal.

15:12 Companies will become loops, and the next step needs a human
The shape of a company is shifting from a list of roles and departments into a cascade of loops: it starts with automating an individual's workflow, then functional loops, then loops that cross business units, until eventually loops run most of the company's operations. The loops themselves keep producing output, and that output becomes the input to the next layer of loops; some mechanism sends the signal back to the CEO — when to adjust the business entity, when the strategy should change. This machinery can help a company climb to a local maximum, but after the plateau it must rely on human intuition to do out-of-distribution thinking and put the organization at the foot of the next mountain. Asking AI to directly come up with a million-dollar idea often fails, because humans can set the right direction while AI only sweeps along a given slope.

32:24 Users want to spend time, not save it
Silicon Valley defaults to AI's value being efficiency; Anish thinks that's a misjudgment: most people don't really want to save time, they want to spend it where it brings connection, love, progress and fun. The biggest products in history have always been entertainment and social, so the consumer opportunity in AI isn't ‘a few more minutes saved’ but building loops that make people feel more connected, more loved, and feel progress or fun. He criticizes the past 40 years of technology for extending intelligence while barely extending the soul; fitting AI into these desires is a product design challenge, not a model capability challenge.

37:29 AI is decoupling skill from desire
Anish sees AI not just as a productivity tool but more like an emotional and spiritual interface — it can split ‘skill’ and ‘desire’ apart. People who want to make music are no longer blocked by ‘I can't play piano’; people who want to write code don't have to first learn enough to hold a job; personal identity is amplified as a result. He looks back at the high-risk environment of the 1950s-60s, which greatly unleashed human potential, and argues today's world is in a low-risk state; AI has a chance to pull GDP growth from 2% to 10-15% — provided what it raises is not the speed of a single step but the scale of what a group dares to imagine.

1:04:42 Ideas that are too small now fail to raise money
Investment criteria have reversed within three years. In the past, if a project was too ambitious, funds would often say a $100 million seed round was absurd; today, looking at deals at a16z, the standard has flipped — if an idea can still only be that small even with AI's help, they simply don't invest. ‘Unbounded ambition’ has become the core value for screening companies; Marc Andreessen's version is: we either go to the moon, or we leave a moon-sized crater.

1:09:48 Shipping something small every week is how you build product intuition
The most direct advice for product people is the old line: build more things. Find a project you tell no one about, the smaller the better, treat it as a ‘chassis’, run each new model through it, ship the finished thing, discuss it with people — that's the path to building AI intuition. The cadence only needs to be one small release a week; going crazy isn't sustainable. Anish himself used Codex to make a Mother's Day slideshow for his wife: pulling material from texts and the photo album, auto-scoring it, and finally generating 20 pages reviewing their relationship, even digging up old texts from their first date. It's small, but work like this lets you taste AI's ‘moments of delight’ over and over — once you've tasted it, you can't go back.
